boundary: Public-safe portfolio and biographical material only. Never disclose private health, financial, relationship, family, compensation, manager, promotion, account, third-party, or unpublished Microsoft details.

chunks.title: About Aadith
chunks.body:
I design Copilot response experiences at Microsoft and co-founded Owly, where we help marketing teams make on-brand videos with AI. I grew up in Kerala, studied Design at IIT Guwahati, and have crossed India twice by bicycle.

Designing AI people can inspect, direct, and actually use.

I grew up in Kerala and spent a lot of time drawing before I knew design was a job. At IIT Guwahati, I learned to follow a problem beyond a single medium. While studying, I worked with early-stage teams on Web3 products, dashboards, personal branding, and fintech. My final-year thesis followed a year of research into personal financial guidance in India, including conversations with advisers and people trying to make sense of investing. By graduation, ambiguous briefs felt pretty normal.

In 2024, I joined Microsoft to work on Copilot responses. I look at how an answer is structured, where its evidence appears, and how people inspect sources. I also work on how the team evaluates quality. Many disciplines shape the product, so I try to ask useful questions early rather than pretend I have every answer.

In 2025, I started Owly with two friends from school. We changed the buyer and the product as we spoke with customers. That work brought early paid customers and clarified what the tool needs to do: remember the brand while leaving the person using it in control. Some days I work on product strategy. Other days I rewrite a button, fix a demo, or discover that our 'simple' workflow contains twelve new states. Founder life has range.

Outside work, I cycle long distances. I have crossed India twice. The first journey took me north. The second was a government-supported expedition from Kashmir to Kanyakumari in 2025, where I represented Kerala alongside about 150 riders. We covered roughly 4,000 km in 16 days. Stubbornness helps, but food, sleep, support, and honest friends help more.

I do my best work on messy problems that cross team boundaries. I help make the question clear, then build something concrete enough for the team to test.

chunks.title: How Aadith works
chunks.body:
Map the system before the screen: I start by mapping who is involved and what each person can see or change. Then I look for constraints and places where the flow can fail. That keeps me from polishing the wrong screen.

Turn taste into evidence: Interviews, customer conversations, examples, rubrics, and quality checks give a team something sturdier than 'this feels better.' Judgment still matters; it just has to explain itself.

Make the trade-off visible: When a debate stays abstract, I build variants or a working prototype and attach a recommendation. The goal is not more options. It is a clearer decision.

Stay through implementation: I stay close while engineers build the design because loading, accessibility, and real content can expose gaps in a mockup. Knowing enough code helps me spot those gaps and fix low-risk ones with engineering review.

chunks.title: Aadith's timeline
chunks.body:
2020 - Started B.Des at IIT Guwahati: Studied Design at IIT Guwahati. The course taught me to choose the method that fit the problem, even when it took me outside one discipline.

2022 - DaoLens - product design at an early Web3 startup: Joined an early Web3 team at twenty while still studying, moving between product flows, brand systems, fundraising material, and event work. It was my first close look at how quickly a company can change direction when the market disagrees.

2023 - Reachify - research became a product: I reached out cold and interviewed 15-20 active LinkedIn creators. Those conversations shaped an idea-to-publish workflow and a working AI-assisted prototype. A short MVP deadline forced the product to focus on one core job.

2024 - Personal finance thesis and Angel One: For my final-year thesis, I interviewed financial advisers and target users about personal financial guidance in India. I then brought what I learned to a six-month product role at Angel One.

2024 - Microsoft - Product Designer: Joined the Copilot team to improve how people read and verify AI-generated responses across Microsoft 365.

2025 - Owly - Co-founded: Started Owly with two friends from school. Customer conversations led to paid work, which showed us what the product still needed to do.

2025 - Ride for Unity: Represented Kerala in a government-supported ride from Kashmir to Kanyakumari, covering roughly 4,000 km in 16 days with about 150 riders.

2026 - AI design enablement and the Lab: Helped document where AI could support an existing design process without replacing human decisions. I kept testing those ideas in small tools for behaviour, evaluation, accessibility, and the handoff from Figma to code.

chunks.title: Cycling across India
chunks.body:
I've cycled across India twice. At twenty, I rode north from Kerala toward Kashmir on a more independent journey. In 2025, I rode south as part of the government-supported Ride for Unity expedition.

On that first ride, I passed beaches, cities, dry plains, and hills. I ate local food and met people who sometimes treated a tired stranger like family. I no longer have a reliable record of the exact distance or duration. What I remember is how quickly an intimidating route shrank to the next town, then the next.

The 2025 ride was faster and far more structured. About 150 of us rode roughly 4,000 km from Kashmir to Kanyakumari in 16 days, with several stages stretching past 200 km. I represented Kerala and relied on a large support team. Endurance in a group is a different skill from doing everything alone.

At that distance, every day becomes practical: eat, pedal, solve the next small problem, repeat. I used to tell these stories as proof of discipline. These days I think they also prove that stubbornness works better with food, sleep, support, and people who tell you when you are being ridiculous.

Route: Kashmir to Kanyakumari. Distance: 4,000 km. Time: 16 days.

chunks.title: Owly
chunks.body:
I'm building Owly with two friends I've known since school. It uses brand context to help marketing teams make video drafts they can direct, without sanding every brand down into the same AI look.

Role: Co-founder, product & design. Period: 2025 to present. Context: Owly.

Building Owly with friends from school

I started Owly with Adi and Hari, two friends I have known since school. I lead product, design, and customer storytelling. Adi works on the AI systems, and Hari builds the backend and runs operations. The roles are complementary, even when the daily task list is not. Owly brings in brand context, helps shape an idea into a video draft, and lets the marketer revise it without starting over.

The product did not begin here

Owly first explored safer, more personal AI video for children. We cared about the idea, but finding buyers and getting frequent feedback was difficult. In 2025, we shifted to brands and growth teams that needed video more often and had budgets for it. One lesson carried over. Generated media is more useful when it reflects a familiar identity and gives people control over the result.

Producing enough usable video

Ads wear out, formats multiply, and a brief passes through strategy, production, edits, approvals, and publishing before it goes live. We kept seeing that the idea was not always the bottleneck. Producing enough usable versions of it was.

A first draft you can actually direct

Owly reads a brand's website and past creative, then uses that context to generate a video draft. A marketer can ask for changes in plain language, and the editor applies them to the work on screen. We are still improving that loop. We want to speed up the first draft without taking direction away from the person responsible for the brand.

Product principles

Start with context and keep the marketer in control

We use these four principles when deciding what to build.

Learn the brand once: Save the website, product catalog, tone, and past creative so the next brief does not begin with another blank prompt.
Show the plan before the render: Show scripts, storyboards, progress, and approval points before and during a long generation step.
Change a scene, not the universe: Support selective edits and regeneration. Full reruns are expensive in time, compute, and patience.
Make the next brief smarter: Use customer feedback and performance data from earlier work to inform the next production.

What should carry into the next project

We want brand context, product catalogs, past creative, and performance history to carry from one project to the next. For now, hands-on customer work shows us which decisions repeat. Those are the parts we can turn into software. We have not built all of that yet.

Founder titles are suspiciously broad

I lead product design, brand, and customer storytelling. Adi works on the AI architecture, Hari handles the backend and operations, and customers regularly prove our assumptions wrong. My work ranges from interaction flows and prototypes to the website, sales demos, and the words the editor uses when it needs clarification. The job changes every week.

Co-founders: 3
Early paid customers: 8+
Company: Self-funded
Current model: Service + software

Paid work is product research with consequences

We used early customer projects to learn where a polished generation demo stops being a usable workflow: inputs arrive messy, brand rules conflict, approvals take time, and one weak scene should not force a full rerender. Doing some of the work by hand is not the final model. It is how we learn which repeated decisions deserve to become software.

Under the hood, for the curious

The product uses Next.js, React, and Tailwind on the frontend, with FastAPI and Supabase behind it. A Python pipeline coordinates video, voice, and language models; brand context lives in Pinecone; and the editor builds on the open-source Friction project. The stack has changed more than once and will probably change again. We try to keep the product idea steadier than the model menu.

I want to build a tool a creative team would genuinely miss when it is gone.

Aadith V A, Co-founder

chunks.title: Microsoft Copilot
chunks.body:
I design and evaluate Copilot response experiences across Microsoft 365 as part of a large team. My work includes citations, response structure, accessibility, and design engineering.

Role: Product Designer. Period: 2024 to present. Context: Microsoft.

This public version leaves out confidential product visuals, metrics, and implementation details.

An AI answer is only part of the experience

My part in a much larger team is shaping the experience around AI-generated responses. I work with product, engineering, research, quality, and accessibility partners on response structure, source presentation, and review. Most of my attention goes to the small interface decisions between a generated answer and the person reading it.

What I work on

The work is mostly small decisions

These parts of the role show up in reviews, prototypes, and quality evaluation rather than as one standalone feature.

Clarify the response: Use hierarchy so the answer, its sources, and available actions do not compete for attention.
Keep sources close: Place source identity near the relevant claim, with more context available when the reader needs it.
Turn taste into a test: Translate a design concern into reusable criteria and examples the team can review together.
Stay close to implementation: Use prototypes and low-risk presentation-layer fixes to check accessibility and visual fidelity.

01. Where did that answer come from?

I designed citation and reference patterns with the wider team to help people trace generated responses back to source material. We worked through how much source identity and context to show without crowding the answer. The aim was to keep the response readable while making its basis easier to inspect.

Citation flow

Start compact, then offer more source context

We treated a citation as a path from the claim to enough source context for the reader to judge it, while keeping the answer readable.

Show the source: Place a readable source label near the relevant claim without filling the answer with controls.
Preview the context: Show a short excerpt or preview so the reader can judge relevance before opening the source.
Open the source: Let the reader continue into the source when the preview is not enough.

02. Useful parts can still crowd an answer

I contributed to a wider team effort to modernize Copilot responses across layout, source hierarchy, actions, and visual clarity. Much of my part happened in critique and edge-case review, where we worked through how those pieces sat together in the product.

03. Giving 'something feels off' a clearer name

Designers often begin with 'something feels off.' I co-created a UX quality-evaluation framework with the team to turn that reaction into reusable criteria, labeled examples, and regression checks. The framework became operational and surfaced quality issues across multiple response experiences.

04. Some details need a running prototype

Even a careful specification leaves questions once the interaction is running. I use code and near-production prototypes to check those details, then contribute small, low-risk presentation-layer fixes alongside engineering and accessibility partners. The work has included spacing, typography, accessibility, and design-system fidelity.

Review is part of the work

I contribute to formal accessibility and design-spec reviews. The wider process includes recurring critique and cross-functional checks, where partners can raise constraints I may not see. That work is quieter than the final screen, but it belongs in the account of how the team worked.

Sharing methods as we tested them

I helped run an internal initiative that documented how designers were using AI in their work. I organized recurring sessions and demos, and contributed to the supporting website. We shared methods the team had tried, including what still needed work, rather than presenting one finished process.

What I am still figuring out

I am still working through how much source context is useful before it becomes clutter and which quality checks should remain a human judgment. In reviews, I bring concrete examples and ask what breaks with an unusual source or in the accessible version. I work through those questions with teammates who know other parts of the system better than I do.

chunks.title: Angel One
chunks.body:
A six-month UX role near the end of college, working inside a large retail-finance product.

Role: UX Design. Period: Jan to Jun 2024. Context: Angel One.

This public summary leaves out detailed product artifacts, metrics, and feature claims I cannot verify.

Six months at Angel One

Near the end of my final year, I spent roughly six months doing UX work at Angel One. It was my first experience designing inside a large financial-services product, where people need to understand what they are doing before they tap. I do not have enough public material to describe individual features or outcomes here.

Working on finance while researching it

The role overlapped with my final semester and academic research into financial advice. The same questions appeared in both. What does someone need to understand before acting? How should an interface explain risk, cost, and uncertainty? Finance interfaces do not get to hide uncertainty behind a cheerful button.

What I learned

Small decisions matter in finance interfaces

These are the habits the work reinforced for me.

Make the decision legible: A person should understand what they are choosing, what changes next, and where to inspect the detail before committing.
Design for hesitation: Pauses, comparison, and second thoughts are not friction to bulldoze. In financial products, they are often signs that the interface needs to explain more clearly.
Keep hierarchy honest: Primary actions can stand out without hiding risk, cost, or constraints in fine print.
Hand off the edge cases: A neat happy path is not enough. States, validation, and exception behaviour need enough detail to survive implementation.

Timeline: 6 months
Domain: Retail finance
Context: Final semester

The question I kept returning to was simple: can someone tell what will happen before they tap?

Aadith V A

chunks.title: Reachify
chunks.body:
An AI writing and scheduling companion built for one job: helping busy professionals show up consistently on LinkedIn without spending their evenings on it.

Role: Freelance Product Designer. Period: 2023. Context: Reachify, early-stage startup.

A personal brand is a lot of small, repeated effort

Reachify started from a familiar problem: people know they should post on LinkedIn, then reach the end of a full workday with no idea what to say. Over four months, I worked solo across research, information architecture, UI, and a working AI-assisted prototype. I focused the product on the recurring work of finding an idea, writing it, scheduling it, and learning from it.

First, find the people already doing the work

I screened for active LinkedIn creators with roughly 2,000 to 10,000 followers. They had enough experience to have real posting habits, but usually not a team doing the work for them. More than 100 cold messages led to 15 to 20 interviews. People described inconsistent ideas, uncertainty about the algorithm, disconnected tools, limited time, and a hope that their expertise might eventually earn money.

Product structure

One product, four recurring jobs

The research led to four product areas based on the work participants repeated each week.

Create: Generate an idea, shape the writing with tone and category controls, add hashtags, and schedule the finished post.
Engagement: Understand who is responding, where a conversation is growing, and which relationships may be worth continuing.
Analytics: Read follower, impression, and post-level trends without turning every creative decision into a spreadsheet.
Dashboard: Use one dashboard to pick up the next small task instead of rebuilding the workflow across several tools.

Two days is not a lot of time

Partway through the project, the investor timeline left two days for an MVP of onboarding and the Create module. I marked Analytics and Engagement as 'coming soon' and spent the sprint on the path from idea to scheduled post.

Doing the job the product was built for

Alongside the product, I wrote and designed hooks, carousel posts, storytelling formats, and practical templates for Reachify's LinkedIn page. The page grew to 2,000 followers. Posting regularly gave me first-hand experience of the job Reachify was meant to help with.

Timeline: 4 months
Screens: 30+
Interviews: 15 to 20
LinkedIn growth: 2,000

I too face this problem of not knowing what to post and how. Have been trying to build a profile that catches eyeballs and ReachifyMe has been a very helpful tool.

Early Reachify user

chunks.title: DaoLens
chunks.body:
Early startup work across product, brand, and marketing, including a documented two-week sprint for DAO Denver.

Role: Product, brand & marketing design. Period: 2022 to 2023. Context: DaoLens.

The startup where the brief rarely stayed in one lane

I joined DaoLens when I was about twenty and worked across product, brand, and marketing. The surviving work includes onboarding, contributor dashboards, governance-related product work, campaigns, and visual systems. Old drafts use different titles, so I describe the role by the work. I was an early designer doing whatever the product and company needed.

My working range

How product, brand, and marketing overlapped

A product decision often changed what the brand or marketing work needed to explain, and the reverse was true too.

Product: The onboarding and contributor work had to explain unfamiliar Web3 concepts to people who did not already know the vocabulary.
Brand: The visual system had to work for a B2B product, community events, and marketing.
Go-to-market: I worked on event material, social posts, product explainers, and campaigns.
Startup rhythm: Briefs changed quickly, and there was rarely time to wait for every role boundary to become official.

What survives publicly

The DAO Denver sprint has a complete Behance case study. I do not have enough public material to describe the broader product flows in the same detail, so this page stays at role-summary level.

Period: 2022 to 2023
Environment: Early startup

Detailed case study: DAO Denver

My job description changed with whatever the company needed that week.

Aadith V A

chunks.title: Crunch
chunks.body:
Dashboard and data-visualisation work for an analytics product, focused on making complex information easier to read.

Role: Dashboard & information design. Period: 2022 to 2023. Context: CrunchIt.

Making dense data easier to read

Crunch brought me into dashboard and data-visualisation work while I was juggling college, startup, and freelance projects. I organised dense information and made comparisons easier to read in the interface.

I was not the data scientist

I was clear that I did not have deep training in data science and had not built the underlying models. I brought dashboard experience and learned the domain as I worked. My responsibility was how the interface presented evidence, comparisons, status, and uncertainty.

Information-design checklist

Four questions I used in the dashboard work

The visual form changed with the data, but I kept returning to these questions.

A starting point: The page needs a clear first read before it asks someone to inspect charts, filters, and secondary metrics.
A fair comparison: Labels, scales, time ranges, and baselines should make comparison easier rather than quietly steering the conclusion.
Visible uncertainty: Show when data is incomplete or ambiguous instead of presenting every value with the same certainty.
A next question: Give the reader enough context to decide what to inspect next.

What I carried into later work

The project gave me an early set of questions about hierarchy, comparison, and uncertainty. I still use them when working on citations, source panels, and evaluation reports.

Focus: Dashboards
Contribution: Visualisation
Domain: Analytics

chunks.title: Citations
chunks.body:
Designing citation patterns that keep source identity near the relevant claim without crowding the answer.

Area: Response UX / citations. Period: 2025 to present. Status: documented. Treat draft entries as incomplete notes, not documented outcomes.

This public summary leaves out internal visuals, metrics, names, and implementation details.

A citation has to help without taking over the answer

A citation needs to show that a claim has a source and help the reader recognise it without interrupting the answer. My part was working through inline references and the move into more source context with the wider team. Accessibility review sat alongside the visual work.

Design questions

Keep the answer readable and the source easy to inspect

Most of the work was deciding what to show beside the claim and what to leave for the next step.

Show the source: Use a readable source name or type instead of relying on a number alone.
Keep it near the claim: Place the reference near the text it supports so checking the source does not become a separate hunt.
Add context when asked: Let a compact reference open into a short preview, with a route to the source when the reader needs more.
Test the awkward cases: Review how the pattern behaves with more than one source, keyboard navigation, and limited space.

chunks.title: Following a citation
chunks.body:
Exploring how a reader can move from a generated claim into useful source context without losing their place in the answer.

Area: Citations / source context. Period: 2025 to present. Status: documented. Treat draft entries as incomplete notes, not documented outcomes.

This public summary stays at the level of source context and reading flow. It leaves out internal screens, rollout details, and product data.

Opening a source is not the same as finding useful context

A link can open the source and still leave the reader searching for the relevant context. Our design work looked at a more continuous path from the claim to a preview and then into the source, while keeping the answer available.

Reading flow

From claim to source context

The reader should be able to see where a claim came from, judge a short preview, and open the source only when needed.

Claim: Keep the source relationship visible beside the statement the reader is checking.
Context: Show a short excerpt or preview so the reader can judge whether the source is relevant.
Open the source: Let the reader continue into the source while keeping the answer available.

A polished answer can still be wrong

A short preview can make a source easier to inspect without forcing the reader to abandon the answer. In a long file, it can help someone decide whether to keep reading.

chunks.title: DAO Denver

Event identity

Applying the identity across eight formats

Collaboration: With Ans

chunks.title: FlowSense
chunks.body:
A screen-recording review tool that links rubric scores and findings to the frames they came from.

A screenshot cannot show delayed feedback, backtracking, or an error that ends a flow. Reviewing the recording can, but manual findings take time and vary by reviewer.

I turned a UX review rubric into an upload, processing, and report flow. Each finding links to a source frame, so a designer can check the cited moment instead of accepting the score alone.

FlowSense began with a question: could a recorded user flow be checked against a consistent rubric without treating the score as objective truth? I wanted a repeatable first pass without hiding uncertainty behind one number.

It grew from a local model experiment into a monorepo with an upload interface, video processor, shared schemas, storage, frame analysis, and reports. The key change was splitting the model work into two passes. One describes observable interaction events; the other scores those events against the rubric.

I added checks around the score. Issues link to frames. Repeat runs show differences. A truncated analysis can warn but cannot pass. The tool still needs a designer to review the findings and the rubric.

A seven-category weighted rubric returns a score from 0 to 100 and a pass, warn, or block result.
The processor extracts frames, selects visible interaction changes, and keeps fact extraction separate from rubric scoring.
Reports link issues and recommendations back to source frames, then compare repeat runs for regressions.
The processing path uses signed webhooks, nonce replay checks, managed identity, and atomic SQL claims.
The monorepo includes focused tests, CI checks, shared schemas, and a test harness for agreement and release metrics.

Limitation: It depends on configured Azure services and credentials, so it is not a one-click public demo.
Limitation: Local development bypasses authentication. A deployment must re-enable it.
Limitation: The repository has benchmark code but no populated, human-labelled holdout set.
Limitation: If a long recording exceeds the analysis budget, the result can warn but cannot pass.
Limitation: A designer still has to decide whether the rubric suits the product and whether the cited frames support each finding.

The model runs in two passes. One answers 'What happened?' The second scores those facts against the rubric. That split made the findings easier for me to trace than a single prompt did.

Built with: Turbo monorepo, Next.js 15, TypeScript, React 18, Azure SQL, Azure Blob, Azure OpenAI, Entra ID, Express worker, FFmpeg.

chunks.title: Figma Redline Bridge
chunks.body:
A local bridge that lets an AI or script draw measurements, specs, and annotation batches inside Figma.

Figma's Plugin API runs inside its sandbox, so an external tool cannot directly draw into the open file. I wanted a local command path that I could inspect, mainly to stop drawing the same spacing arrows by hand.

The project combines a Node relay, WebSocket connection, plugin iframe, Figma runtime, and commands for drawing annotations. Most of the work sits in the handoffs between those parts.

I began with a narrow test: send a command from an external tool and draw a spacing redline in the open Figma file. Figma's sandbox made that a multi-step route.

The local relay turns an HTTP request into a WebSocket message, passes it through the plugin iframe with postMessage, and calls the Figma API. Replies travel back along the same route. I added commands for spacing, dimensions, colour, typography, page creation, and ordered batches.

The project later expanded into documentation experiments, but the bridge remains the part I care about. It automates repetition without claiming to automate taste. A person chooses what needs an annotation; the tool draws it.

A four-hop command path connects HTTP clients to a Node relay, WebSocket, plugin iframe, and Figma sandbox.
Remote commands cover spacing, dimensions, colour, typography, page creation, and ordered batches.
The server queues commands while Figma is disconnected and exposes connection state through a health endpoint.
The plugin preserves auto-layout by rescaling cloned frames rather than mutating dimensions directly.

Limitation: The localhost command endpoint is unauthenticated and should not be exposed beyond a trusted local machine.
Limitation: Only one active Figma client is supported; a new connection replaces the previous socket.
Limitation: Batch commands fail when Figma is disconnected instead of joining the normal pending-command queue.
Limitation: Setup still requires a server process, a plugin build, and a manually loaded Figma development manifest.
Limitation: There is no automated test suite for the cross-runtime message path.

Drawing a line was straightforward. Moving a command through three runtimes and Figma's sandbox without breaking auto-layout was not. A plain protocol made the route easier to debug.

Built with: Figma plugin, TypeScript, Node.js, WebSocket (ws).

chunks.title: Behavior Diff
chunks.body:
A word-level before-and-after view of one prompt, constraint, or input change.

A small change to a prompt, policy, or context can produce a very different response. Two full outputs side by side make those differences hard to locate.

The prototype allows one changed variable per scenario, so each comparison stays tied to a specific prompt, constraint, or input edit.

Agent changes can look small in configuration and much larger in the response. I wanted a code-style diff that marks added, removed, and unchanged wording instead of reducing the comparison to a better-or-worse score.

The prototype has three controlled scenarios. One changes the response requirements, one adds a VIP constraint, and one changes the incoming message. A custom word-level diff feeds both split and unified views, so both modes show the same comparison.

The rerun is simulated and the outputs are authored fixtures. That let me work on the comparison interface before building live model runs. The views have not yet been tested with variable, non-deterministic output.

Three fixtures each change one thing: the response requirements, a VIP constraint, or the customer's message.
A custom longest-common-subsequence engine computes word-level additions, removals, and unchanged spans.
Split and unified views share one diff result, with line alignment and empty rows keeping comparisons legible.
The interface also shows change counts, the exact configuration difference, and a simulated rerun state.

Limitation: The outputs are authored fixtures; the rerun button does not call a live model.
Limitation: All three scenarios use customer support, so the prototype has not been tried across other domains.
Limitation: Configuration is visible but not editable, so new experiments still require code changes.
Limitation: There is no backend, persistence, automated test suite, or committed deployment.

If I change three things and compare two outputs, I learn almost nothing. Each scenario therefore names its one changed variable before showing the red-and-green diff.

Built with: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Framer Motion.

chunks.title: System Messages
chunks.body:
A field guide to confirmations, boundaries, access notices, and other chat messages that should not sound like the assistant.

Designing system notices one at a time leads to inconsistent treatment as a chat product grows. Confirmations, session boundaries, access notices, errors, and ordinary UI changes begin to look and sound alike.

I kept the interface quiet so the classification and rules carry the page. It groups system messages into four categories and documents when to use each one, how it behaves, and how to write it.

System messages record facts inside a chat: an action finished, a session ended, a visibility rule starts here, or the whole conversation has a special access condition. They belong to neither the user nor the assistant, but they affect how someone reads the timeline.

I grouped them into four categories and added a decision tree for a harder question: when should there be no system message at all? Assistant output, service errors, and ordinary interface changes need different treatment. Narrating every state change adds noise.

The prototype is a field guide, not an app. One page documents message parts, placement, persistence, timing, interaction, and writing rules. It also gives a team a shared vocabulary and a way to reject messages that add no information.

Four categories cover action acknowledgements, session lifecycle markers, context boundaries, and conversation-wide access notices.
A decision tree distinguishes system messages from assistant output, application errors, and UI state changes.
Each category documents anatomy, placement, persistence, timing, interaction, and content rules.
The public prototype includes a sidebar, table of contents, examples, and a single-page reading path.

Limitation: The site documents the classification and rules; it has no authoring workflow or component playground.
Limitation: Examples omit internal product scenarios, policy, and visual tokens.
Limitation: The taxonomy still needs broader scenario testing to expose ambiguous or overlapping cases.
Limitation: The prototype has no search, contribution model, version history, or automated documentation tests.

The rule I kept returning to was simple. If a state change adds no information, leave it in the interface instead of announcing it in the conversation.

Built with: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4.

chunks.title: Agent Canvas
chunks.body:
A Figma-like canvas for mapping an agent's steps, decisions, responses, and quality criteria.

Agent behaviour is often split across prompts, configuration, and orchestration code. That makes product decisions hard to see, critique, or hand off.

I wanted agent behaviour to be something a team could inspect together. The prototype maps steps, decisions, responses, and weighted quality criteria on one canvas.

We could draw a user flow, write a prompt, or make a prototype, but none put an agent's turn-by-turn behaviour in one place. I sketched a node-based canvas that borrows from Figma without treating conversation as a simple flowchart.

Each scenario uses typed steps. Selecting one opens its instruction, output, and quality criteria in the inspector. Preview replays a short simulated conversation and highlights the active message and canvas node together.

The interface is ahead of the implementation. The drag handles do not work, edits disappear on refresh, and the preview is hard-coded. I built enough interaction to ask whether a designer, PM, and engineer could discuss the same behaviour on the canvas.

Three sample scenarios model onboarding, file analysis, and error recovery as connected five-step flows.
The canvas uses four step types: trigger, action, decision, and response.
Quality criteria carry must, should, and nice-to-have weights rather than sitting in a separate checklist.
Preview mode replays a simulated conversation and highlights its active canvas node.

Limitation: The preview currently replays one hard-coded scenario rather than compiling the flow being edited.
Limitation: Edits live only in local component state; refresh the page and they are gone.
Limitation: Dragging, adding steps, and some toolbar controls appear in the interface but do not work yet.
Limitation: There is no agent backend, persistence layer, automated test suite, or deployment yet.

The prototype exposed a more immediate gap than persistence: Preview does not compile the flow being edited. Until it does, the canvas and conversation are linked demonstrations, not one authoring tool.

Built with: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Framer Motion, Lucide React.

chunks.title: Conversation Pattern Library
chunks.body:
A searchable library of six conversation patterns, with guidance, anatomy, and replayable examples.

Teams often solve the same conversation problems inside separate mockups: clarifying an ambiguous request, revealing complexity gradually, recovering context, and confirming a risky action. The reasoning rarely travels with the design.

The library records repeated conversation decisions together with the situations and limits that determine when each pattern applies. It currently contains six patterns.

I designed the library around a practical task: find a pattern for a specific situation, understand its limits, and follow it across several turns. The chat bubbles come after that.

The library contains six patterns: Clarification Loop, Progressive Disclosure, Graceful Fallback, Escalation to Human, Destructive Action Confirmation, and Context Recovery. They share one data schema, which drives search, category filters, anatomy diagrams, guidelines, and replayable examples.

Six patterns are a starting set, not a full design system, and there is no contribution workflow yet. Related patterns also need links because one conversation may use several.

Six authored patterns span clarification, disclosure, error handling, handoff, and confirmation.
Every pattern includes when-to-use guidance, principles, four anatomy steps, a conversation example, and tags.
Search matches names, descriptions, and tags; category filters update the visible library count.
Live Preview, Anatomy, and Guidelines views let the same pattern be read as an example, a structure, or practical advice.

Limitation: The library contains six patterns and is not a comprehensive system.
Limitation: Patterns are static TypeScript data with no authoring, review, or contribution workflow.
Limitation: There are no deep links to a selected pattern, and browser history does not capture exploration.
Limitation: Related patterns are mentioned but are not modelled or linked in the interface.

This build documents when each pattern applies and where it stops. It does not yet link patterns that often appear in the same conversation.

Built with: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Framer Motion.

chunks.title: AI made prototyping cheap. It did not make judgment cheap.
chunks.body:
I have not found a separate 'AI design process' useful. I still try to understand the context and define the problem before I make an idea tangible and test what happens. AI can help with parts of that work, but it does not make any stage optional.

Synthetic personas can help me find better questions before research. They cannot validate a need or reproduce the strange specificity of a real conversation. AI summaries can cluster messy notes, but evidence and product context still determine what those clusters mean. The people affected by the decision still need a say.

AI saves me the most time when I turn an idea into something people can try. I now move from a rough flow to a code prototype before polishing a static specification. A working interaction exposes problems that a still screen can hide. Once it works, I still need to resolve the states, accessibility, spacing, and implementation details.

A running prototype can still be unsafe or incomplete. Security, data protection, edge cases, and compliance need deliberate work. So does the interface. Sometimes I can help by making a small code fix and asking an engineer to review it. Sometimes the right call is to keep the prototype out of production.

I am wary of large prompt libraries that nobody has tested. The number of prompts says little about whether they help in real work. I would rather test a small set in real scenarios and gather feedback. If an entry does not hold up, I remove it before publishing the library.

AI can produce more options. I still have to explain which one holds up and why.

chunks.title: System messages are part of the conversation.
chunks.body:
Some of the most important messages in a chat come from neither the user nor the assistant. A system message might confirm that an action finished or mark the end of a session. It might also explain a visibility boundary or an access condition. These messages are small, but they change what a person thinks just happened.

It is tempting to design each message as a one-off. That falls apart when several teams give the same event different words and visual treatments. I found it more useful to classify each message by its job before writing it.

A useful classification also needs to say what does not count. When an assistant completes a request, that is chat output. A network outage is an application error. An ignored suggestion that collapses is interface behaviour. If a change tells the user nothing new, another message usually adds noise.

A system message should read like a receipt, not another speaker in the chat. One sentence is usually enough. It does not need an avatar or conversational padding. Messages that record an event should remain in the timeline. A general reminder can disappear only if the same information remains easy to find elsewhere.

If a state change communicates nothing new, it probably does not need another message.
